name: Browsertrix and the WARC standard. Two coupled things. THE STANDARD: WARC (Web ARChive) file format, ISO 28500:2017, maintained in practice through the IIPC's warc-specifications (current WARC 1.1); its predecessor the Internet Archive ARC format; and the WACZ (Web Archive Collection Zipped) packaging format that bundles WARCs with an index, page list and datapackage manifest for direct browser replay. THE TOOLS: Browsertrix (Webrecorder's hosted, browser-based crawling service), browsertrix-crawler (the open-source Docker-packaged crawler driving Chromium via Puppeteer and the Chrome DevTools Protocol), ArchiveWeb.page (the manual, extension-based capture tool), and the replay side -- ReplayWeb.page and wabac.js, plus pywb and OpenWayback as the classic replay servers. Contrasting crawler: Heritrix, the non-browser-based Internet Archive crawler that WARC was originally designed around.
kind: A standard (ISO 28500 / WARC), a packaging convention (WACZ), a service (hosted Browsertrix), and open-source tools (browsertrix-crawler, ArchiveWeb.page, ReplayWeb.page). Not a benchmark and not a research result, though the archiving community has produced fidelity studies about it (see item 10).
maturity: The most mature item in this research set. WARC has been an ISO standard since 2009 (revised 2017), is the format of national library and Internet Archive holdings measured in petabytes, and has multi-decade institutional commitment behind it. Browsertrix is production and actively developed, and represents the current state of the art in browser-based (as opposed to fetch-based) capture; it is what memory institutions increasingly use for the dynamic web that Heritrix cannot handle. WACZ is younger and is a de-facto convention driven by Webrecorder rather than a formal standard, though it is widely adopted in that ecosystem. Nothing here is experimental.
license: Favourable overall with one wrinkle. The WARC standard itself is an ISO document that must be purchased, but the IIPC publishes the specification openly and a draft is freely available from BnF, so the format is implementable without buying anything. browsertrix-crawler is AGPL-3.0, which carries the same network-service obligation flagged for SingleFile in item 1 and should be checked before integration -- running it as an external process is the usual way to keep the boundary clear. ReplayWeb.page and wabac.js are AGPL-3.0 as well. pywb is GPL-family. The warcio and warcat-style Python libraries are permissive (warcio is Apache-2.0), which matters because reading and writing WARC does not require touching the AGPL tools at all. Hosted Browsertrix is a commercial service under its own terms. PRACTICAL CONCLUSION: adopt the FORMAT freely using permissive libraries; treat the Webrecorder TOOLS as AGPL components to be invoked rather than linked. [uncertain] on the exact licence of every component in the Webrecorder stack.
keeps_and_discards: WARC's design decision is the important one and it is different in kind from every other capture approach in this research set: it keeps the HTTP EXCHANGE, not the rendered page. A WARC file is a sequence of typed records -- ISO 28500 defines eight types: warcinfo, response, request, resource, metadata, revisit, conversion and continuation -- each with an HTTP-like header block and a content block. A response record holds the complete protocol response including headers and entity body; a request record holds the outgoing request including its body; a revisit record notes that a previously archived resource is unchanged WITHOUT storing the payload again, which is the format's native deduplication mechanism; conversion records store a derived version together with details of the transformation, which is a first-class provenance construct for transformed data; continuation splits oversized records across segments. What this keeps that nothing else does: the exact bytes the server sent, with the exact headers, for every resource, plus the requests that elicited them. What it discards: the RENDERED result. A WARC does not contain a DOM, does not contain computed styles, does not contain the post-JavaScript page. Replaying one requires re-executing the page against the archived responses, which is what wabac.js and pywb do and which is where fidelity is actually won or lost. Browsertrix additionally captures screenshots, extracted text and page metadata alongside the WARCs, precisely because the exchange alone does not answer 'what did this look like'.
structure_preserved: At the exchange level, completely: every resource, its URI, its headers, its status, its timing and its relationship to a request. Origin boundaries are preserved exactly -- unlike SingleFile's inlining, a WARC keeps each third-party resource as a separate record with its own target URI, so 'which of this came from an ad network' is directly answerable, and that is a substantial and under-remarked advantage for provenance and for governance. At the DOCUMENT level, nothing is preserved beyond the HTML bytes as delivered: no DOM, no shadow roots, no post-hydration structure. So a WARC of a client-rendered application contains an empty shell plus a pile of JavaScript and JSON, and the structure exists only after replay re-executes it. Browsertrix mitigates this by capturing the XHR and fetch traffic the page makes during its instrumented visit, so the data the page needed is in the archive; the structure still has to be reconstituted by running the page.
interactive_elements: Controls are preserved as whatever markup and script the server sent, so they are FUNCTIONALLY LIVE on replay in a way no other capture in this research set manages -- clicking a button in ReplayWeb.page runs the page's real handler, and if the resulting request was captured, the interaction works. That is the strongest fidelity claim available and it is why browser-based archiving exists. Its limit is coverage: only interactions whose network dependencies were captured during the crawl replay correctly, so a form submission, a search, or a lazily-loaded page-two that the crawler never triggered will fail on replay. Browsertrix addresses this with behaviours -- scripted simulated browsing activity (scrolling, clicking, expanding) that provokes the page into making the requests worth capturing -- which is an explicit, configurable, and inherently incomplete answer to an unbounded problem.
interactive_state_fidelity: Not represented at all in the archive, and not needed in the same way, because state is reconstructed by re-execution rather than serialised. A WARC does not record that a checkbox was checked; it records the resources that let the page run, and the page's own logic determines state on replay. That is a genuinely different model from every markup- or AX-tree-based approach and it has a corresponding weakness: the replayed state is whatever the page's scripts produce from the archived responses, which may not be what the crawler saw, and there is no record of what the crawler saw to compare against except the screenshots Browsertrix takes alongside. Token cost is not an applicable axis; nothing here is model-facing.
layout_awareness: The FORMAT is layout-free -- WARC records are bytes and headers with no geometric content whatsoever. The TOOLS are layout-aware: Browsertrix runs a real Chromium, its behaviours scroll and interact based on rendered state, and it captures screenshots. So the split falls exactly where this project's constraint wants it: the stored artifact contains no geometry, and the capture process consumes geometry to decide what to fetch. That is a useful precedent -- geometry used as an actuator to drive capture, never stored in the record.
javascript_required: For the crawler, yes and that is the whole point: browsertrix-crawler runs a real browser via Puppeteer and CDP precisely so that script-generated requests are captured, and it is described as producing near-full-fidelity copies including server-dependent parts by simulating browsing activity. ArchiveWeb.page is noted as more successful than non-browser-based tools such as Heritrix at the cost of requiring manual operation. For REPLAY, the archived page's own JavaScript must run against a rewritten network layer, which is where most replay failures originate. For READING a WARC as data, no JavaScript is needed at all -- the records are parseable with warcio and similar libraries, which is the mode most relevant to this project.
evaluation_method: The archiving community's method is REPLAY-BASED: capture, replay, and compare the replayed page against the live one, usually by human inspection and increasingly by automated visual comparison. This is the only fidelity evaluation tradition in this research set with an institutional constituency behind it, and item 10 (the IMC 2025 archiving-fidelity work) is where the quantitative version lives. Format conformance is separately checkable against ISO 28500 with validators. Browsertrix's own quality signals are operational -- crawl completion, page counts, error logs, and the screenshots and extracted text it stores alongside, which function as a within-archive oracle. What is NOT systematically evaluated anywhere: how much of a dynamic page's behaviour survives replay, expressed as a rate over a real corpus, which is precisely the gap item 10 addresses and which the tooling community historically treated qualitatively.
corpus_size_and_origins: Not a research artifact with an evaluation corpus, but the deployment corpus is by far the largest in this set: WARC holdings at the Internet Archive and national libraries run to hundreds of petabytes across billions of origins and three decades. That breadth is real but it is not a controlled corpus -- it is an accumulation, with unknown and heterogeneous capture quality, crawler versions, and policies. Browsertrix-specific holdings are much smaller and much newer, concentrated in institutions that adopted browser-based crawling recently, and skewed toward exactly the dynamic sites that motivated the switch. For this project the relevant reading is that WARC's format-level robustness is proven at extreme scale, and its fidelity-level performance is not characterised by any figure that could be quoted.
reported_precision_recall: No precision/recall figures exist for the format and none would be meaningful. The format-level guarantees are exact rather than statistical: a response record contains the bytes that were received, byte-for-byte, with digests (WARC-Block-Digest and WARC-Payload-Digest) that make tampering or corruption detectable. The fidelity-level figures belong to item 10. Two qualitative claims recur in the tooling documentation and should be labelled as vendor-adjacent rather than measured: browsertrix-crawler produces near-full-fidelity copies including server-dependent parts, and ArchiveWeb.page has been noted as more successful than non-browser-based tools such as Heritrix. Both come from Webrecorder or from community write-ups about Webrecorder tools; neither is a controlled comparison, and the second is a comparison against a tool designed for a different era of the web. [uncertain] -- no independent quantitative comparison of Browsertrix against alternatives was located.
independent_oracle: Several, and this is one of the format's strengths. (1) The DIGEST fields (WARC-Block-Digest, WARC-Payload-Digest) let any reader verify that a record's content is what was originally written, independent of the writer -- content integrity is checkable without trusting the archive. (2) The REQUEST records paired with response records let a reader verify that a response was actually elicited by a plausible request rather than fabricated. (3) Replay in an independent implementation (pywb versus wabac.js versus a raw record read) tests whether an archive is well-formed independently of the tool that wrote it. (4) Browsertrix's screenshots stored alongside the WARCs are an independent visual record against which a replay can be checked -- a genuinely good design decision that most archiving pipelines lack. What has no oracle is the counterfactual: whether the archived exchange is what a different visitor at the same moment would have received, which personalisation, A/B testing and geolocation all make uncertain and which no archive can answer.
evidence_independence: The STANDARD is a multi-institution ISO document with no single vendor's interest in it, which is as independent as a specification gets. The TOOLS' fidelity claims come from Webrecorder, which builds and sells them, and should be read accordingly. The archiving research community (IIPC members, national libraries, the Old Dominion web-science group whose orphan study appears in item 23) does produce independent evaluations of archived-content fidelity, and item 10 is where those numbers live. Nothing in the present item's descriptive claims about record types or format semantics is vendor-sourced -- they come from ISO 28500 itself.
page_archetype_coverage: Uneven in a way the community understands well. Static article, documentation and news archetypes capture and replay near-perfectly and are what WARC was designed for. Application-shell and single-page-application archetypes are the hard case: they capture as a shell plus scripts plus API responses, and replay correctly only if the crawler provoked the right API calls, so coverage depends entirely on the behaviours configuration. Listing and infinite-scroll archetypes capture only as far as the crawler scrolled. Service, transactional and authenticated archetypes are largely out of reach -- a crawl cannot complete a checkout, and capturing behind a login requires credentials and raises its own issues. Media-heavy pages capture but are enormous. Anything relying on live third-party services (maps, embedded players, real-time feeds) replays partially or not at all because the service is not in the archive. The failure is graceful in that the page still renders; the missing parts are silently absent, which is the community's known pain point.
script_and_locale_behaviour: Format-neutral: WARC stores bytes with declared content types and character sets, so it is script-invariant by construction and preserves whatever encoding the server sent, including malformed or mislabelled encodings, exactly as received -- which is the correct archival behaviour. Browsertrix's text extraction and its behaviours are the locale-sensitive parts: scripted interactions that look for particular UI patterns are language-dependent to the extent they match on text, and text extraction inherits whatever the extractor does with CJK segmentation and RTL. No measurement of non-English capture quality was located. [uncertain].
leaks_outward: A crawl is a crawl: it is fully visible to the origin, generates a recognisable request pattern, and identifies itself by user agent (browsertrix-crawler sets an identifiable UA by default, which is deliberate good practice). It fetches every subresource by design, so third parties learn of the visit. Hosted Browsertrix additionally means the crawl runs from Webrecorder's infrastructure and the operator's target list is known to that service. Manual ArchiveWeb.page capture runs from the operator's own browser and session, which changes the disclosure profile entirely -- and means captures can include authenticated content, with all the consequences that implies. This is the honest, non-covert end of the capture spectrum, and the tools do not pretend otherwise.
mechanism_detectability: High and largely by design. browsertrix-crawler drives Chromium through the Chrome DevTools Protocol, which carries a well-documented detection surface (the CDP-detection arms race is a separate item in this research set), and it identifies itself in its user agent rather than hiding. The crawl request pattern is recognisable. ArchiveWeb.page runs as a browser extension and inherits extension-detectability. None of this is a defect for the intended use -- memory institutions crawl openly and want to be identifiable so that operators can allowlist them -- but it means the whole stack is unusable as a covert sensor, and the contrast with the undetectable in-page DOM read of item 26 is stark. For this project the transferable point is architectural: the Webrecorder stack has chosen legibility over stealth, and its governance posture (below) follows from that choice.
countermeasures: Not adversarial hardening but archival robustness, and the mechanisms are worth naming because several are directly reusable. Digests for integrity. Revisit records for deduplication without loss of the record that a resource was seen. Conversion records to make transformation explicit rather than implicit. Continuation records to handle oversized payloads without truncation. WACZ packaging with an index and a datapackage manifest so an archive is self-describing and its contents enumerable without a full scan. And on the crawl side, configurable behaviours plus explicit crawl scoping to bound what is fetched. Against the fidelity problem specifically the countermeasure is capture-side rather than storage-side: run a real browser and provoke the page, which is exactly what Browsertrix does and exactly why it exists.
measured_fidelity_cost: Not measured within this item; the quantitative work belongs to item 10. What can be said structurally: the cost of browser-based capture over fetch-based capture is orders of magnitude in time and infrastructure (one Chromium per worker versus a socket) in exchange for capturing the dynamic web at all; the cost of storing the exchange rather than the render is that replay is required and can fail; and the benefit of storing the exchange is that a single archive supports many different derivations (extract text now, re-extract with a better extractor later) which a rendered snapshot does not. That last property is the one this project should weigh most: an exchange archive is a REPROCESSABLE source, a rendered snapshot is a fixed derivation.
gate_state_at_capture: Partially and unusually well handled, which is worth noting because almost nothing else in this research set records it at all. Because a WARC stores the full HTTP exchange including status codes, redirects, Set-Cookie headers and the request headers sent, the gate state is largely RECONSTRUCTIBLE from the archive: a 401 or 402 is in the record, a redirect to a login page is in the record, a consent-management response is in the record, and whether cookies were carried is in the record. That is a strictly better position than any DOM- or markdown-based capture, which sees only the resulting page. It is not annotated as a field -- nobody stamps 'this capture was behind a paywall' on the warcinfo record -- but the evidence is preserved, and adding a metadata record asserting the gate state is exactly the sort of thing the metadata record type exists for. This is a concrete, standards-blessed pattern the project could copy.
determinism: The format is deterministic and self-describing: a WARC written once reads identically forever, and digests make that checkable. The CAPTURE is not deterministic -- two crawls of the same site produce different archives because the site differs, because behaviours interact nondeterministically with page timing, and because network conditions change which resources arrive. REPLAY is the least deterministic stage, since it depends on the replay implementation, on the browser executing the archived page, and on whether the page's scripts take paths whose dependencies were not captured. So determinism decreases monotonically down the stack: format high, capture low, replay lowest.
determinism_across_versions: The format is stable across decades -- WARC 1.0 files written in 2009 are readable today, which is the strongest cross-version stability in this research set and is the direct result of it being an ISO standard with institutional commitment. Replay is the unstable layer: an archived page's rendering depends on the browser used to replay it, so a 2015 capture replayed in a 2026 browser renders differently from how it rendered in 2015, and this is a known and unsolved problem in the archiving community (the browser is not archived along with the page). Browsertrix's own output evolves with releases. The practical lesson for this project mirrors the one everywhere else: record the tool version and the browser build, and expect the RENDER of a stored artifact to drift even when the artifact does not.
reproducibility: This is the format's central virtue and the reason it appears in this research set. A WARC freezes the exchange, so every downstream derivation can be recomputed from it: extract text now with one extractor, re-extract in two years with a better one, and both runs are reproducible against identical bytes. That is exactly the property item 23's orphan study identified as missing (archive the target at the time you record something about it), that item 25's change-detection literature lacked, and that this project's own corpus currently lacks, with 75% of its pages fetching live resources on every read. If there is one thing to take from this item it is the format's implicit thesis: STORE THE EXCHANGE, DERIVE EVERYTHING ELSE. The corresponding limitation is that reproducibility of the exchange does not give reproducibility of the RENDER, because the browser is not archived.
failure_modes: (1) INCOMPLETE CAPTURE of dynamic dependencies -- the crawler did not provoke a request, so replay fails for that interaction; the dominant failure and the reason behaviours exist. (2) REPLAY BREAKAGE from URL rewriting: replay systems must rewrite absolute URLs, intercept fetch/XHR, and virtualise storage APIs, and pages that construct URLs dynamically, use service workers, or check their own origin can defeat this. (3) LIVE-LEAKAGE during replay, where a replayed page successfully reaches the live web for something not in the archive, silently contaminating the archived view with present-day content -- a well-known and serious archiving problem. (4) PERSONALISATION AND GEOLOCATION making the captured exchange unrepresentative. (5) UNCAPTURABLE CONTENT: authenticated areas, POST-dependent responses, streaming media, WebSocket traffic, WebRTC. (6) SCALE: WARCs are large, and without revisit-record deduplication the same resource is stored per capture. (7) CDP and browser instability under long crawls. (8) The replay browser problem noted above.
failure_visibility: Mixed and better than most. Crawl-side failures are loud: browsertrix-crawler logs errors, records failed pages, and the archive's page list makes coverage enumerable. Format-level corruption is detectable via digests. But the two failures that matter most are silent: a page that replays MOSTLY correctly with a missing region gives no signal that anything is absent, and live-leakage produces a page that looks perfect precisely because it fetched the missing piece from the present-day web. The archiving community's mitigation for the second is strict network isolation during replay, which must be configured deliberately. For this project the transferable rule is the same one recurring throughout: an archive should carry an explicit manifest of what it FAILED to capture, and WACZ's datapackage is the natural place for it.
scale_limits: Storage scales with total bytes fetched, which for browser-based capture means every subresource of every page, and the format's built-in economy is the revisit record -- a previously archived unchanged resource is referenced rather than re-stored, which is content-addressed deduplication in all but name and is why petabyte-scale WARC holdings are feasible at all. Crawl throughput scales with browser instances: browsertrix-crawler runs multiple PageWorker instances within a single browser process in a Docker container, which is the pragmatic answer, but the floor is still roughly one browser tab per concurrent page, orders of magnitude heavier than Heritrix's socket-per-fetch. Indexing (CDX/CDXJ) is what keeps lookup sublinear and is the reason WACZ bundles an index. Replay cost is a full browser per replayed page.
delta_cost_model: The format has a genuine and well-designed delta mechanism at the RESOURCE level and none at the page level. The REVISIT record is exactly a per-change storage model: when a resource is re-crawled and found unchanged (established by payload digest or by HTTP validators), a revisit record is written referencing the earlier record instead of storing the payload again, so storage cost is proportional to CHANGED bytes rather than to fetched bytes. That is the closest thing to O(delta) in this research set outside the trie itself, it is standardised, it is deployed at petabyte scale, and it is directly worth copying. What falls OUTSIDE that bound and must be named: (1) the FETCH is still performed in full -- revisit saves storage, not bandwidth or time, so crawl cost remains O(page) even when nothing changed; (2) detecting no-change requires either a digest computed over the fetched bytes (so the fetch happened) or trust in HTTP validators (ETag, Last-Modified) which many servers get wrong; (3) there is no sub-resource delta -- a one-byte change to a large file stores the whole file again, since WARC has no diff or chunk-level record type; (4) the rendered result has no delta representation at all, so two captures of a page whose DOM changed slightly are two complete archives; (5) index rebuild cost as the collection grows; (6) nothing in the format is aware of DOM-level change, so this mechanism is orthogonal to, not a substitute for, mutation-driven incrementality.
reanchoring_stability: The addressing scheme is (URI, capture timestamp), which is the Memento model and is coarse but extremely durable -- a URI-plus-datetime pair survives everything a DOM address does not, because it identifies a RESOURCE rather than a position within one. There is no sub-document addressing in WARC at all, so re-anchoring within a page is entirely outside the format's scope and must be layered on (the W3C Web Annotation selectors of item 23 are the natural pairing, and TimeState in that model exists precisely to reference a Memento). The transferable design point is that the project's url:xpath key is the composition of exactly these two levels -- a durable resource identifier and a fragile intra-document position -- and the archiving world's experience is that the first level is worth treating as a separate, stable, timestamped identity rather than as a prefix string.
adversarial_exposure: An archive preserves everything the server sent, including concealed content, injected payloads and malicious scripts, byte for byte -- which is correct archival behaviour and makes a WARC the best forensic record in this research set: an injection can be located in the exact response that carried it, with its headers, its origin and its timestamp. Note the direct synergy with item 13's finding that 54.5% of in-the-wild indirect prompt injections live in HTTP RESPONSE HEADERS, including purpose-built fields such as X-AI and X-LLM: a WARC is the only capture format here that stores those headers at all, so it is uniquely able to measure that class, and conversely a DOM-based fold never sees them (which is protective for consumption and blinding for analysis). Two hazards. First, replaying an archived hostile page executes it, so replay must be sandboxed and network-isolated; live-leakage during replay is both a fidelity and a security problem. Second, an archive is a durable store of malicious content, which is a handling obligation rather than a defect. Nothing in the format filters concealment and nothing should -- the value is in preserving it for inspection.
provenance_carrying: The best in this research set, by a clear margin, and it is worth cataloguing because several mechanisms are directly copyable. Every record carries WARC-Record-ID, WARC-Date, WARC-Target-URI, WARC-Type, Content-Type and digest fields; warcinfo records carry file-level provenance including the software that produced the capture and crawl details; request records pair with responses so the eliciting request is preserved; metadata records attach arbitrary descriptive information to other records WITHOUT a payload, which is a general-purpose annotation hook; conversion records make derivation explicit by recording that this content is a transformation of that content, together with details of the transformation; and revisit records preserve the fact that a resource was observed at a time even when its bytes are not re-stored. Crucially, per-resource origin is preserved rather than erased -- the opposite of SingleFile's inlining. The two things missing relative to this project's needs are sub-document addressing and any notion of shadow depth, both of which are outside the format's level of description. The CONVERSION RECORD is the most transferable idea: a first-class, standardised way to say 'this artifact is derived from that one by this process', which is exactly what a projection needs and which nothing else in this research set provides.
roundtrip_safety: Read-write round trips are exact by design: records are length-delimited byte sequences with digests, so parse-and-rewrite is a fixed point and any deviation is detectable. That is the correct model for an archival container and is much stronger than the ad-hoc serialisation stability elsewhere in this set. The lossy round trip is CAPTURE-REPLAY-RECAPTURE, which is not a fixed point and is not expected to be, since replay reconstructs rather than reproduces. Escaping is not an issue at the container level -- payloads are opaque bytes -- which is itself a design lesson: making the container binary-safe and length-delimited removes an entire class of escaping bugs that text-delimited formats have.
token_budget_and_ordering: Not a model-facing format, and this is the right way for it to be. A WARC is a source artifact from which model-facing projections are derived; it should never be tokenised. Its relevance to the token contract is indirect but real: because the archive is reprocessable, the projection's budget and shape can be changed and re-derived later without recapturing, which is the property that makes budget experimentation possible at all. A pipeline that stores only its projection has frozen its budget decision permanently.
representation_cost: Storage is the full byte weight of everything fetched, mitigated by revisit deduplication across captures and by compression (WARCs are conventionally gzip-per-record, which preserves random access). This is the heaviest storage format in the set per capture and the lightest per capture-after-the-first, because of revisit records. Compute cost is a browser per page for capture and a browser per page for replay. What is bought is the ability to re-derive any other representation, which is the highest-value property for a long-lived corpus and the lowest-value one for a real-time sensor.
what_could_be_adopted: Six mechanisms, none requiring the AGPL tools. (1) STORE THE EXCHANGE, DERIVE EVERYTHING ELSE. This is the format's thesis and it directly answers the reproducibility defect this project has -- 75% of its corpus fetching live resources on every read means no measurement over that corpus is re-derivable. Freezing the responses makes every downstream figure recomputable and every regression diagnosable. (2) THE REVISIT-RECORD DEDUPLICATION MODEL: when a re-fetch yields an unchanged payload (by digest), store a reference rather than the bytes. Standardised, proven at petabyte scale, and directly applicable to repeated captures of the same page. Its named limitation -- it saves storage, not fetching -- must be carried with it. (3) THE CONVERSION RECORD as a first-class derivation record: every projection, every downsampled artifact, every sanitised text should record what it was derived from and by what process, in a form a reader can follow back. Nothing else in this research set offers this and the project needs it for exactly the audit trail its provenance design implies. (4) THE METADATA RECORD as a payload-free annotation hook attachable to any other record -- the natural home for gate state, capture conditions, tool versions and declared-incompleteness flags, and a better pattern than stuffing them into the artifact itself. (5) PER-RESOURCE ORIGIN PRESERVATION, in explicit contrast to SingleFile's inlining: never merge third-party content into first-party content without keeping the boundary, because governance, injection analysis and data-protection questions all need it. (6) DIGESTS ON EVERYTHING, making integrity checkable by any reader without trusting the writer. Explicitly NOT to be adopted: browsertrix-crawler as the capture mechanism (AGPL, CDP-detectable, self-identifying user agent, one browser per page, no DOM-level output); and the assumption that capturing the exchange gives you the page, which is exactly the assumption that made browser-based archiving necessary in the first place.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism: ADOPTABLE AS-IS. WARC stores bytes and headers and makes no judgement about content structure; it names no regions and classifies nothing. Browsertrix's BEHAVIOURS are the boundary case -- scripted interactions that scroll and click to provoke requests are heuristics about page structure, and to the extent they match on UI patterns or text they are exactly the kind of pre-computed structural assumption the constraint forbids. VERDICT: format adoptable as-is; behaviours ADOPTABLE IN THE ACTUATOR LAYER ONLY, since provoking a page is an actuator function and its heuristics never enter the fold. no_layout_in_the_fold: ADOPTABLE AS-IS for the format, which contains no geometry. The crawler consumes layout to drive behaviours and to take screenshots, which is actuator-side, and this is a good precedent for the split the project wants: geometry used to decide what to capture, never stored in the record. o_delta: PARTIALLY ADOPTABLE AND A GENUINE CONTRIBUTION. The revisit record is a standardised, deployed per-change STORAGE model and should be adopted. It is not a per-change CAPTURE model: the fetch is still full, detection of no-change requires the fetch or trust in HTTP validators, there is no sub-resource delta, the rendered result has no delta representation, and the format is entirely unaware of DOM-level change. Those five exclusions must accompany any claim built on it. no_mocks: ADOPTABLE AS-IS and exemplary -- real browsers, real network, real bytes, with digests proving the bytes are unaltered. The fidelity CLAIMS ('near-full fidelity', 'more successful than Heritrix') are vendor-adjacent and unquantified and should be treated as NEGATIVE ORACLE ONLY until item 10's measurements are consulted. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: NO CONFLICT AND AN INTERESTING PROPERTY. WARC never touches the DOM, so the closed-root question does not arise at capture; on replay, closed roots are reconstructed by the page's own code exactly as they were originally, which means the boundary is honoured by construction. This is the only capture approach in the set that sidesteps the question entirely rather than negotiating it. OVERALL VERDICT: the FORMAT is adoptable as-is and is the strongest single design influence available here -- store the exchange, use revisit records for delta storage, conversion records for derivation, metadata records for gate state and incompleteness, and keep per-resource origin. The TOOLS are rejected as a capture mechanism for this project on licence, detectability and cost grounds, and their behaviours belong strictly to the actuator layer.
governance_signal_handling: The most governance-conscious item in this research set, and the norms are institutional rather than technical. browsertrix-crawler identifies itself with a distinctive user agent by default and supports robots.txt handling and configurable crawl scoping, rate limiting and politeness delays; the memory-institution community that drives these tools has decades of practice negotiating access, honouring exclusions, and operating under legal-deposit or permission regimes rather than unilaterally. The choice to be identifiable rather than stealthy is deliberate and is what allows operators to allowlist archival crawlers -- a genuine, working example of governance by legibility. Newer signals (Content Signals, ai.txt, AIPREF, Web Bot Auth, HTTP 402) are not yet reflected in the tooling as far as this research found, and there is an unresolved tension the community is actively discussing: archival crawling and AI-training crawling look similar to a server and are increasingly blocked together, so archival access is collateral damage in the AI-crawler backlash. [uncertain] on the current state of AIPREF or Content Signals support in browsertrix-crawler. Because a WARC stores the full exchange including the robots.txt fetch and any 402 or 403 responses, the governance interaction is itself archived, which is a good property.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: The archiving world has the most developed practice here of anything in this set, and it is instructive. WARC holdings are typically justified under legal deposit, library and archive exceptions, public-interest archiving provisions, or explicit permission, rather than under an ad-hoc legitimate-interest claim -- and GDPR's Article 89 research-and-archiving provisions plus national legal-deposit legislation are the usual footing. The corresponding practices are access control (many archives capture broadly and restrict access narrowly, sometimes to reading rooms), embargo periods, and takedown procedures. Two format-level properties help: metadata records give a standardised place to attach retention class, legal basis and takedown status to any record, and the URI-plus-timestamp addressing makes prefix- and time-scoped deletion tractable. Two properties hurt: an archive of the full exchange contains everything including personal data in headers, cookies and payloads, and it is by design permanent, which is in direct tension with storage limitation and erasure. Manual capture with ArchiveWeb.page from an operator's own logged-in session is the highest-risk mode, since it captures authenticated third-party personal data under the operator's credentials. The transferable practices are: separate the capture decision from the access decision, attach retention metadata at capture time, and make gate state explicit. [uncertain] on any specific analysis under EDPB Guidelines 03/2026, which is item 19's subject; note that guidance aimed at generative-AI scraping may treat an archival justification quite differently from a training one, and the two must not be conflated.
